$comment: Shared route-composition table: the exact source each bundler emits for a
route's element tree and its loading shell.
Both bundlers generate a client entry, and a project renders through
whichever one built it:
- crates/ruvyxa_bundler/src/output.rs        (`build`, `preview`)
- packages/ruvyxa/runtime/entry-templates.mjs (`dev`, and the SSG path)
Composition order is the whole contract. The boundary sits inside the
Suspense so a synchronous throw renders its own UI rather than making React
emit the loading fallback; the layouts wrap outward root-to-leaf; the
metadata is a sibling of the layouts rather than a wrapper, so a layout that
suspends cannot hold the document title back past the flushed shell. A
bundler that reordered any of those still produces a page — a differently
behaved one, only on the half of the deployments that used it.
Every implementation replays this file:
- crates/ruvyxa_bundler/src/output.rs                    (Rust test)
- tests/packages/ruvyxa/entry-prelude-parity.test.mjs    (JavaScript test)
An intercepting route is emitted as `__ruvyxaSlot(ctx, level, name, Default,
table)` rather than as a fixed element, because the overlay is decided per
render from `ctx.intercept` and the slot may have no default of its own. A
route with no interceptions emits exactly what it always did, which the
earlier cases here still pin.
$normalizationNote: Compared with statement terminators removed. The Rust literals are written
with semicolons and the JavaScript templates without them — Prettier owns
the second and neither reaches a reader, so a byte comparison would fail on
the formatting while passing on a reordered composition. Each side strips a
`;` that ends a line before comparing, which is why no `routePath` in this
$namesNote: The Rust generator hardcodes the identifiers it emits; the Node generator
takes them as arguments. These are the values that make the two agree.
`layoutWrappers` is the already-joined list both sides interpolate.
